appraisal_events.evidence: Rachel, jadis « une grue qu'on laissait figurer dans les pièces », est « devenue une actrice célèbre », récite chez la princesse de Guermantes, a « décidément Rachel pour amie » du côté de la duchesse, et le bruit court dans Paris « que c'était Rachel qui, en réalité, recevait chez la princesse ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage stages Rachel's completed social ascent as an accomplished fact: she is intimate with the duchesse de Guermantes, is the drawing card of the matinée, and is spoken of as its real hostess. The narrator ironizes the mechanisms of the rise but not the reality of it, and registers his own displeasure at it, which confirms rather than undercuts her new standing.

appraisal_events.evidence: Chez la Berma « les heures passaient et personne n'arrivait » ; « il y avait vide absolu et mort » ; on s'assied « comme pour un repas funéraire » ; elle a « la mort sur le visage », et son unique invité finit par partir vers les Guermantes.
appraisal_events.explanation: The abandoned tea party inflicts a total local social defeat on la Berma: her faithful desert her for the rival attraction, and the narrator frames the scene as a funeral. Her artistic genius and her contempt for Rachel are preserved, but they are exactly what the world now ignores.

status_effects.explanation: Rachel moves from remembered kept woman and bit-player to celebrated actress, friend of the duchesse, and de facto hostess of the most desired gathering in Paris.
Her guests defect en masse to the Guermantes matinée, leaving her house empty; the world's verdict inverts the hierarchy she herself still upholds.
Dying, exploited by her daughter and son-in-law, and publicly deserted, she is left with only a murmured, powerless expression of contempt.

Her intimacy with Rachel becomes evidence against her: the new generations conclude that despite her name she must be « quelque demi-castor qui n'avait jamais été tout à fait du gratin » and read her position as lower still.

Rachel's elevation reaches Gilberte as a snub by proxy: her aunt's « vive antipathie » makes receiving her late husband's former mistress a pleasure, and the sight of Rachel triumphant is one the narrator must shield her from.

ambiguities: The bare form « princesse de Guermantes » is registry-ambiguous, but here it is determinately Mme Verdurin: she is the aunt whose « mésalliance » with Gilberte's uncle is mocked, and she claims to have known Odette and introduced her to Swann.

The narrator explicitly leaves the duchesse's intimacy with Rachel underdetermined between two opposed readings — vindication of her anti-snob sincerity, or proof of a mediocre, unsatisfied intelligence — so the direction of her personal appraisal is genuinely open even though the social verdict against her is not.
